hook: A microwave oven heats leftovers, an infrared camera sees body heat, and ultraviolet light gives you a sunburn. All three are light, differing only in wavelength, and each does something different to molecules. Chemists use that to identify substances with light alone.

prereq.q: In photoelectron spectroscopy, what does a photon do to an atom?
prereq.why: A high-energy photon can remove an electron from an atom.
O and H differ in electronegativity.

figure.caption: The electromagnetic spectrum and the molecular change each region causes.

chain.cause: Shorter-wavelength light carries more energy per photon
chain.effect: radio < microwave < infrared < visible < ultraviolet < X-ray in energy

chain.cause: Molecules hold energy in fixed levels: rotation (small gaps), vibration (medium), electronic (large)
chain.effect: a photon is absorbed only if its energy matches a gap

chain.cause: Each region matches a different kind of gap
chain.effect: microwaves rotate molecules, infrared vibrates bonds, visible and UV light promote electrons

chain.cause: The levels depend on the atoms and bonds present

ideas: Shorter wavelength, higher frequency, more energy per photon.
Microwave: rotation. Infrared: vibration. Visible and UV: electronic transitions. X-ray: core electrons removed.
A photon is absorbed only if its energy matches the gap between two levels.
A colored substance absorbs some visible light; we see the light it does not absorb.

misconception.wrong: Brighter light of any color can always push an electron to a higher level, if there is enough of it.
misconception.right: Each photon must carry energy matching the gap. Many low-energy photons cannot add up to one electronic transition.

summary: Electromagnetic radiation ranges from radio waves to X-rays; shorter wavelengths carry more energy per photon. A molecule absorbs a photon only when its energy matches a gap between levels: microwaves change rotation, infrared changes vibration, and visible and ultraviolet light move electrons to higher levels. Spectroscopy uses these absorptions to identify substances.
